extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and legal scholars (patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and equitable principles governing the grant or denial of preliminary and permanent injunctions in patent infringement actions, including what proof, conduct, and circumstances justify or bar injunctive relief. Extracts cover evidentiary modes, laches/estoppel, territorial/contractual exceptions, and discretionary equity considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of proof to establish infringement for injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Where the identity has already been established in prior actions, the judgments therein rendered may be offered … If the invention is an instrument, and the defendant has in his possession or under his control the alleged infringing articles, the court may personally inspect and compare them, and without further proof determine their substantial agreement or dissimilarity. When these modes of investigation are unavailable, such evidence must be introduced as the plaintiff is able to obtain.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Use prior adjudications, physical inspection/comparison of accused devices, or whatever evidence plaintiff can obtain. Cases cited: Crowell v. Harlow; Morse Fountain Pen Co. v. Esterbrook; many others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to practise / readiness as evidence of threatened infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The intention of the defendant to practise the invention must be determined anew upon each motion for an injunction … The intention of the defendant to practise the invention, or preparations to infringe, may be shown from his past acts of infringement, or from his threats or preparations to infringe.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Past infringement, threats, preparations, possession of infringing machines, or indications of ability/readiness are competent evidence of intent and justify injunctive relief. See Brooks v. Miller, Gutta Percha & Rubber Hfg. Co. v. Goodyear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction may issue on threatened, not yet committed, infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That an injunction will be granted if defendants feel disposed, before a wrong is committed when the right is clear and the wrong is threatened, or when the wrong has once been committed and there is good reason to fear its repetition.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Courts may issue anticipatory injunctions where plaintiff’s right is clear and threatened harm is likely. See Sherman v. Nutt; Poppenhusen v. New York Gutta Percha Comb Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of infringement immaterial for preliminary injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘For the purposes of a preliminary injunction the extent of the defendant's infringement is immaterial.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Even limited or prospective infringement can justify a preliminary injunction if other requirements are met. Cases: Brickill v. Mayor of New York; Pullman v. Baltimore & Ohio R.R. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction need not be supported by proof beyond reasonable doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That an injunction may be granted though infringement is not proved beyond reasonable doubt.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Lower standard of proof may suffice for preliminary relief; equity focuses on threatened injury and balance of convenience. Example: Doughty v. West.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to exhibit accused device raises presumption of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That the refusal of a defendant to exhibit his device raises a presumption of infringement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: If defendant will not produce the device for inspection, court may draw an adverse inference. Cases: Piper v. Brown; Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Binney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disputed infringement may be settled by inspection/comparison without prior adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That disputed infringement may be settled by inspecting the two devices without any prior adjudication.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: For preliminary determinations courts can compare devices in court to resolve infringement disputes. Cases: Crowell v. Harlow; White v. Harris & Sons Mfg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patented process is a continuing infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That the use of an invention involving a patented process is a continuing infringement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Process patents give rise to continuing violations as long as the process is practiced. Citation: Beedle v. Bennett.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession/advertising of infringing articles and profit are relevant to injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Assertions of his right to practise the invention, the possession of infringing machines capable of operation or of marketable articles covered by the patent, or other indications of ability and readiness to enter into unlawful competition … are competent evidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Possession/advertising and commercial use/supporting profits weigh in favor of injunctive relief. Examples: Woodworth v. Hall; Union Paper Bag Mach. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction may issue notwithstanding denial of plaintiff's title
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That an injunction may issue notwithstanding a denial of the plaintiff's title.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Even where defendant contests plaintiff’s title, equity may enjoin infringing acts pending further adjudication where necessary to prevent harm. See Clum v. Brewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior adjudicated questions treated as settled on injunction motion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That on a motion for an injunction all questions adjudicated in previous cases are regarded as settled.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Issues already litigated and decided are given preclusive effect in injunction proceedings; see Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Evans and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable injury requirement for injunction (grounds for refusal)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Among the reasons relating to the plaintiff which may induce the court to refuse an injunction is the fact that no irreparable injury would result from the infringement. Thus where the patent is about to expire, or an established license fee exists and has been tendered by the defendant, or the damages resulting from the infringement could be easily computed and the defendant is pecuniarily responsible … the court may either deny the application or grant it in modified form.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Courts may deny/preclude or tailor injunctions when monetary relief is adequate — e.g., near-expiry patents, license tendered, easy-to-compute damages, defendant solvent. Cases: Pullman Car Co. commentary; Westinghouse Air Brake Co. v. Carpenter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's laches/acquiescence can bar preliminary injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Another reason is found in the plaintiff's acquiescence in the infringement, or his laches in the enforcement of his rights … An intelligent and voluntary consent, even though manifested only by inaction, for any considerable period, if unexplained, is a fault that may deprive him of a remedy in equity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Long delay, failure to enforce rights, abandonment of invention, or allowing general unlicensed use without attempting to restrain may preclude injunctive relief. Examples and citations: Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.; Wyeth v. Stone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay may not be laches if satisfactorily explained
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That delay in bringing actions against infringers, when satisfactorily accounted for, is not to be treated as laches.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Explanations such as patentee’s bankruptcy, vesting in assignee, or other reasonable causes can excuse delay. Cases: Green v. French; McLaughlin v. People's R.R. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's duty to notify known infringers; notice suffices if given as able
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The owner of a patented invention owes a certain duty to known infringers, which obliges him to give them notice of the wrongful character of their use … Having given this notice without avail, he may postpone his suit during the pendency of other actions, or during any reasonable time upon sufficient cause, provided no intentional encouragement is afforded to the infringers.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Timely notice to infringers is required; mere forbearance after notice does not bar injunctive relief absent affirmative encouragement. Cases: Kittle v. Hall; Collignon v. Hayes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence of prior owners binds assignees (laches runs with title)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That the plaintiffs are chargeable with the laches of former owners of the patent … An assignee of claims for past infringements is bound by the laches of his assignor.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Successor holders inherit defenses of laches/estoppel based on prior owners’ conduct. Cases: Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.; N.Y. Grape Sugar Co. v. Buffalo Grape Sugar Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel where plaintiff’s conduct misled defendant into enterprises
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Where the laches or acquiescence of the plaintiff has misled the defendant into enterprises which would be destroyed by an injunction, the court will recognize the estoppel and refuse the desired relief.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: If defendant reasonably relied on plaintiff’s silence/inaction and undertook significant investments, equity may deny injunction due to estoppel. Cases: various (cited in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of infringer from past liability does not bar future injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That the release of an infringer from liability for the past is no bar to an injunction for the future.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Even where past conduct has been released, courts can enjoin ongoing/future infringement. Cases: Babcock & Wilcox v. Pioneer Iron Works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad faith by patentee or inequitable conduct can defeat injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Where the plaintiff has violated his equitable obligations to the defendant … if the defendant is a licensee and has been secretly under-sold by his licensor … or if any subsisting relation between the parties renders the interference of the court unjust, the application for an injunction will be denied.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Fraudulent licensing, secret underselling, or other inequitable conduct by patentee may preclude injunctive relief. Cases: Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. v. Scutt; Hoffheins v. Brandt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may withhold injunction for public or relational equities/new difficult questions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That no injunction will be granted where new and difficult questions are to be decided, or where there is anything in the relations of the parties which could cause it to operate unjustly.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Complexity, novelty, or risk of inequitable impact on parties/public may counsel denial or deferral of injunction. Example: Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Binney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions may be limited to allow fulfillment of existing contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Acts of bad faith toward the public may also furnish reasons for denying an injunction … the injunction, although general in reference to all other uses of the invention, may except this contract from its operation and permit him to fulfil it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Courts can craft injunctions that carve out obligations to third parties entered in good faith so that essential contracts can be performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting a license may preclude injunction where license exists or tendered
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Where the plaintiff grants licenses the injunction may be refused and a license fee ordered … That where the license fee exists and is tendered, an injunction will be denied.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: If licensing or tender of license fees would adequately protect plaintiff’s interests, equity may award monetary remedy or license instead of injunction. Cases: Blake v. Greenwood Cemetery; Smith v. Sands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction is discretionary and governed by equitable principles
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Whenever … it is apparent that the plaintiff has a right which the defendant threatens to invade, an injunction may be issued — the rules which govern the discretion of the court being intended for the furtherance of justice, not for its denial. But where one or all of these three forms of proof are offered, it is still within the same discretion to withhold relief, for reasons which indicate that its application in the present instance would be inequitable. These reasons relate to the situation and conduct of the plaintiff or defendant, to the substance of the patent, or to the consequences which would follow from the grant of an injunction.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Courts balance rights, conduct, patent substance, and consequences; issuance of preliminary relief is an equitable decision. See entire §1192 discussion.
